contributions.headingText: Endometrial atypical hyperplasia / endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia (EAH/EIN) is simultaneous change of epithelial cytology and an increased number of endometrial glands in comparison with the stroma (crowded gland architecture) within a morphologically defined region, distinct from the surrounding endometrium or from entrapped normal glands.
GA16.0 & XH4Z68 Endometrial glandular hyperplasia & Endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia
Not recommended: complex atypical endometrial hyperplasia; simple atypical endometrial hyperplasia; endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia
The average patient age is 50–55 years. Postmenopausal or perimenopausal bleeding is the most common presenting symptom.

Hereditary susceptibility parallels that of heritable syndromes associated with increased risk for endometrioid endometrial carcinoma, including Cowden syndrome and Lynch syndrome {23239812; 19078925}.

EAH/EIN emerges as a clonal expansion of mutated glands that begins as a localized lesion and may expand to occupy the entire endometrial compartment {10699996}. EAH/EIN contains many of the genetic changes seen in endometrioid endometrial carcinoma {11389050}. These include microsatellite instability (including Lynch syndrome); PAX2 inactivation; and PTEN, KRAS, and CTNNB1 mutation {20631067; 12635138}.

Many lesions have no distinguishing macroscopic features; others present as a focal thickening resembling a polyp, or within a diffusely thickened endometrium {19851198}. The gross appearance is often obscured by hyperplasia without atypia, endometrial polyp, or carcinoma.

EAH/EIN is composed of crowded aggregates of altered tubular or branching glands, cytologically distinct from the background architectural and cytological pattern {3385513}. In an area of EAH/EIN, the glands exceed the stroma, which leads to a reduction of the stromal volume. The lesion must be of sufficient size (admittedly a subjective measure) that artefact can be excluded and coincident change of architectural and cytological alterations is evident. Nuclear appearance varies between patients but is always distinct from that of the background from which the lesion has emerged. Cytoplasmic changes (various types of metaplasia) may accompany nuclear atypia in EAH/EIN {18637968}. Common mimics (basalis, polyp, dyssynchronous-phase endometrium) must be excluded. Endometrial hyperplasia without atypia and EAH/EIN can be distinguished on the basis of a combination of architectural features (whole-field vs geographical, respectively) and cytological features (uniform field vs changed from background, respectively) {7074572; 7694941}. Loss of immunoreactivity for PTEN, PAX2, or mismatch repair proteins may be a helpful diagnostic tool {20631067; 14614055; 31186530}.

Essential: morphologically defined endometrial changes with crowded glandular architecture and altered epithelial cytology, distinct from the surrounding endometrium and/or entrapped non-neoplastic glands.

Desirable: loss of immunoreactivity for PTEN, PAX2, or mismatch repair proteins.

One quarter to one third of women with a biopsy of EAH/EIN will be diagnosed with cancer at immediate hysterectomy or during the first year of follow-up {16400639}. Longer-term risk elevation estimates vary from 14-fold in earlier 4-class hyperplasia studies to 45-fold in 2-class endometrioid intraepithelial neoplasia studies {4005805; 21691159; 20065186}. The efficacy of conservative treatment of grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma or EAH/EIN with hormonal agents may be monitored by histology, but this is not yet standard clinical practice {31846531}.
